Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Review the types of hematopoietic bone tumors.
Define the histopathologic findings and diagnostic criteria associated with myeloma and
lymphoma.
Describe the classic radiographic appearance of myeloma and lymphoma.
Explain the clinical presentation of patients with a hematopoietic bone tumor.
Discuss the medical and surgical management of hematopoietic bone tumors.
Introduction
Lymphoma and multiple myeloma are malignancies of the hematopoietic cell lineage. Both
derive from cells of varied stages of development within the lymphocytic cell line. Because

Bone marrow involvement may lead to remodeling of the medullary and cortical trabeculae,
which eventually may cause to weakening of the bone and pathologic fracture.
Myeloma is derived from mature B lymphocytes.
Lymphoma is derived from T or B lymphocytes or natural killer lymphocytic cells at different
stages of maturation.
Multiple Myeloma
Pathoanatomy/Pathophysiology
Overview
Definition and demographics
Neoplastic proliferation of plasma cells producing a monoclonal protein
Most common primary malignant bone tumor (30,000 individuals/year) in the United States
Primarily affects patients older than 40 years
Twice as common in African Americans compared with Caucasians
Affects males more commonly than females.

Overview
Multiple myeloma is the most common primary bone malignancy in the United States
(Resource 1). The disease is characterized by neoplastic plasma cells and tends to affect
marrow spaces. Patients with multiple myeloma commonly have bone manifestations.
Epidemiology
Approximately 3% of patients older than 50 years
Approximately 98 cases/1 million individuals
Rare in younger populations


Epidemiology
Multiple myeloma represents approximately 1.8% of all malignancies in the United
States, accounting for approximately 18% of all hematologic malignancies. More than
30,000 individuals in the United States are diagnosed with multiple myeloma each year,
which equates to an annual age-adjusted incidence of approximately 98 cases/1 million
individuals. Although the incidence of multiple myeloma has not changed substantially in
recent decades, modest improvements in survival have resulted in an increase in the
overall prevalence of multiple myeloma in the past 20 years. Multiple myeloma is slightly
more predominant in males and is two to three times more common in individuals of
African descent. The median age of patients with multiple myeloma is approximately 70
years; however, at the time of diagnosis, 37% of patients are older than 75 years and
37% are younger than 65 years. Multiple myeloma is rare in patients younger than 40
years.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Bone manifestations are frequently observed.
Lesions occur throughout the skeleton but are common in bones that contain hematopoietic
marrow, including the skull, spine, and long bones (Figure 1).

Figure 1 AP radiograph of the hip of a 47-year-old woman demonstrates a pathologic fracture of
the proximal femur through a lytic lesion. Open biopsy performed at the time of surgical
management revealed a plasma cell neoplasm consistent with plasmacytoma/multiple myeloma.
(Reproduced from Weber KL: Malignant bone tumors, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive
Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp
1560-1586.)

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The bone manifestations of multiple myeloma often are clinically and radiographically
important. The disease primarily involves the red marrow, with subsequent trabecular
bone resorption. Therefore, the most common sites of disease in adults are those rich in
red marrow, including the spine, skull, pelvis, ribs, proximal femur, and proximal
humerus. Bone disease may present as a large lytic lesion or multiple so-called punched
out lesions throughout the bone. Fractures and impending fractures can occur in any
bone and contribute to disease-related pain. The surgical approach for skeletal disease
is similar to that for metastatic disease: the risk for fracture is related to the location and
size of lesions and activity-related pain.

Etiology
Genetics/etiology
Immunoglobulins (Igs) are composed of two heavy chains and two light chains.
Heavy chains: IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, and IgE (IgG and IgA are common in myeloma)
Light chains: kappa and lambda (Bence Jones proteins)
Myeloma produces heavy and light chains.
Major mediators of osteoclastogenesis in myeloma include receptor activator of nuclear
factor-kappa B ligand, interleukin-6, and macrophage inflammatory protein-1 alpha.
Osteoblastic bone formation is suppressed by tumor necrosis factor and Dickkopf-related
protein 1.

Etiology
In patients with skeletal lesions, the increased production of multiple cytokines
(interleukin-1 beta, interleukin-3, and interleukin-6) helps promote osteoclastic
differentiation and growth factors (tumor necrosis factor- alpha, hepatocyte growth
factor, and vascular endothelial growth factor), supporting osteoclast survival and bone
resorption.
Although many tumor-related osteolytic processes are accompanied by a compensatory
attempt at remodeling via osteoblastic bone formation, myeloma bone disease typically
is characterized by a combination of increased osteoclastic resorption and suppressed
bone formation. Patients with multiple myeloma have increased expression of Dickkopf-
related protein 1 and soluble frizzled-related protein 2, both of which are inhibitors of
Wnt signaling, a key pathway for osteoblast differentiation. Enhanced osteoclastic bone
resorption in combination with inhibited osteoblastic bone formation strongly favors
osteolysis in patients with skeletal lesions from multiple myeloma, contributing to the
radiolucent appearance of myeloma bone lesions.
Immunoglobulins are composed of two heavy chains and two light chains. In patients
with multiple myeloma, heavy chains (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, and IgE) and light chains (kappa
and lambda) may be produced. IgG and IgA are the most common heavy chains in
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:21 PM
AAOS | Hematopoietic Bone Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004046
5/38

patients with multiple myeloma. The light chains may manifest as Bence Jones proteins,
which may be detected in the urine of some patients.
Natural History
Progression of disease from monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined clinical significance
(MGUS) to smoldering (or asymptomatic) myeloma to symptomatic multiple myeloma
In 70% of patients, smoldering myeloma will progress to symptomatic multiple myeloma
within 15 years.
Solitary plasmacytoma is a single identified site of malignancy without evidence of plasma or
urine light chains.

Natural History
In most patients, multiple myeloma is thought to progress from MGUS to smoldering or
asymptomatic myeloma and ultimately to symptomatic multiple myeloma. MGUS has
been noted in approximately 3% of individuals older than 50 years. A diagnosis of MGUS
confers a small but persistent risk of progression to multiple myeloma.
Smoldering myeloma is considered an intermediate stage in the progression of multiple
myeloma. The rate of progression to multiple myeloma is highest early in the diagnosis
of smoldering myeloma. Symptomatic multiple myeloma will develop in approximately
70% of patients with smoldering myeloma within 15 years.
Solitary plasmacytoma, which is a similar disease process, manifests as a single
identifiable tumor of malignant plasma cells, with no evidence of multiple myeloma
observed on imaging studies, marrow biopsy, serum tests, or urinary analysis.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History

Common symptoms include bone pain, pathologic fracture, and recurrent infection.
Spinal disease is common and may cause pain, deformity, fracture, and spinal cord
compression.

Patient History
Bone pain is a common symptom in patients with multiple myeloma. Given the overlap
in age distribution, multiple myeloma consistently is included with metastatic carcinoma
and lymphoma in the differential diagnosis for a lytic bone lesion of unknown origin in
patients older than 40 years (Resource 2). The non-osseous clinical features of multiple
myeloma may be extensive, including renal dysfunction, anemia, infection,
hyperviscosity, bleeding, and hypercalcemia. Prompt recognition of these symptoms,
particularly spinal cord compression, renal dysfunction, and hypercalcemia, is critical
because emergent management may prevent severe or life-threatening complications.
Physical Examination
Variable physical examination findings
Tenderness
Pain on resisted activity
Some patients may have back pain or spinal cord compression on initial presentation.
Patients with advanced disease may have signs of end-organ damage.
Hypercalcemia
Gastrointestinal disturbance
Neurologic/mental status changes
Pain
Muscle cramps
Increased thirst
Anemia
Renal dysfunction
CRAB symptoms
Hypercalcemia

Renal insufficiency
Anemia
Bone lesions
POEMS syndrome is less common.
Polyneuropathy
Organomegaly
Endocrinopathy
Monoclonal protein spike
Skin changes
Patients with POEMS syndrome may have sclerotic lesions rather than the typical lytic foci.

Physical Examination
Patients with a lytic lesion who may be at risk for a pathologic fracture may have aching
pain or tenderness. In patients with mechanical insufficiency of the bone who may be at
risk for a pathologic fracture, pain with weight-bearing activity is concerning.
Patients with lytic lesions in the spine or compression fractures may have back pain or
spinal cord compression on initial presentation.
Patients with advanced disease may have signs of end-organ damage. Hypercalcemia
may manifest as gastrointestinal disturbance, neurologic or mental status changes, pain,
muscle cramps, or increased thirst.
POEMS syndrome is a less common manifestation. POEMS syndrome includes
polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal protein spike, and skin
changes. Although purely lytic lesions typically are observed in patients with myeloma
bone disease on initial presentation, patients with POEMS syndrome may have sclerotic
bone lesions. On the radiographs of some patients, sclerotic bone lesions may have an
appearance similar to that of a blastic carcinoma metastasis, as observed in prostate
carcinoma.

Imaging Studies
Overview
Classic appearance is multiple punched-out lytic lesions throughout the skeleton (Figures 2, A
and B; and 3, A).
Typically, no surrounding sclerosis; lesions may develop a sclerotic rim after management.
Skull lesions and vertebral compression fractures are common (Figures 2, A; and 3, A).
Diffuse osteopenia (Figure 3, A)

round, punched-out lesions of multiple myeloma. (Reproduced from Weber KL: Malignant bone
tumors, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1560-1586.)

Overview
The classic radiographic findings of multiple myeloma are characterized by focal,
osteolytic lesions without a sclerotic rim (Resource 3). Lesions generally begin centrally
in the marrow; however, with enlargement of the tumors, endosteal scalloping, cortical
destruction, fracture, and a soft-tissue mass may develop. Osteolytic foci often are well
circumscribed, with a sharp zone of transition. In the skull, they are described as
punched-out lesions. In some patients, multiple myeloma may result in a more diffuse
pattern of osteolysis, which may mimic senile osteoporosis or adopt a permeative

destructive appearance. After systemic management, lesions often develop a thin
sclerotic rim, which may aid in determining chronicity (Video 1).
Video 1 Levin AS: Adult bone tumors and pitfalls, from Morris CD: Bone and soft tissue
tumors for the general orthopaedic surgeon: How to diagnose, manage, and avoid
errors. Presented a the Annual Meeting of the American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, Las Vegas, NV, March 12-16, 2019.
Radiography
Skeletal survey
Radiographs of the skull, chest, spine, pelvis, humeri, and femora
Detects approximately 80% of myeloma lesions
Useful in predicting fracture risk

Radiography
Historically, a skeletal survey was used to screen for osseous disease in patients
with multiple myeloma. A skeletal survey includes AP and lateral radiographs of
the spine (cervical, thoracic, and lumbar), humeri, femora, and the skull; PA
radiographs of the chest; and AP radiographs of the pelvis. Additional areas
should be imaged based on symptomatic involvement. A lesion is detectable on
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:21 PM
AAOS | Hematopoietic Bone Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004046
11/38

skeletal survey in approximately 80% of patients with a new diagnosis of
multiple myeloma.
Bone Scintigraphy
Detects 35% to 60% of skeletal lesions.
Bone scintigraphy may be negative or may underrepresent the extent of disease
because of minimal osteoblastic response in myeloma.

Bone Scintigraphy
On initial presentation, multiple myeloma often is included with metastatic
carcinoma and lymphoma in the differential diagnosis for a lytic bone lesion.
The typical workup for a patient with a skeletal lesion suspicious for metastatic
carcinoma involves technetium-99m bone scintigraphy to identify additional
sites of disease. Because bone scintigraphy involves the use of technetium-99m,
it is a marker of bone formation, which is not characteristic of myeloma bone
disease in patients without a pathologic fracture. This imaging modality detects
35% to 60% of skeletal lesions from multiple myeloma and is less sensitive and
less specific than a skeletal survey. Therefore, technetium-99m bone
scintigraphy is not included in the standard evaluation of the extent of bone
involvement in patients with multiple myeloma.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Whole-body MRI is the imaging modality most sensitive in identifying osseous lesions
in patients in whom multiple myeloma is suspected.
Preferred imaging modality for evaluation of suspected solitary plasmacytoma
MRI helps characterize vertebral lesions.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging

AAOS | Hematopoietic Bone Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004046
12/38

Whole-body MRI is slightly more sensitive in identifying skeletal lesions in
patients with multiple myeloma and is particularly beneficial in identifying and
characterizing vertebral lesions. Diffusion-weighted MRI help distinguish
marrow signal change from marrow-replacing plasmacytoma. Whole-body MRI
is the preferred first-line imaging modality for the evaluation of a suspected
solitary plasmacytoma of bone.
Positron Emission Tomography/CT
Positron emission tomography (PET)/CT currently is the preferred imaging modality.

Positron Emission Tomography/CT
With a sensitivity and specificity of approximately 85% and 90%, respectively,
fluorodeoxyglucose-PET/CT is associated with better identification of skeletal
lesions compared with radiography in approximately one-half of patients with
multiple myeloma. The detection of lesions smaller than 1 cm is limited with
PET/CT, and PET/CT fails to detect a lesion identified on MRI in 30% of patients,
most commonly in those with diffuse marrow involvement. Typically, PET/CT is
performed from the head to the mid-thigh; therefore, specific efforts to include
PET/CT of the legs may be appropriate. Although whole-body MRI is more
sensitive than PET/CT at the time of diagnosis, PET/CT best detects minimal
residual disease after management.
Pathology
The lesion consists of sheets of plasma cells with eccentric nuclei.
Little intercellular material (matrix) is present with extensive vascularity (Figure 3, B).
Nuclear chromatin arranged in a clock face pattern
Immunohistochemistry (IHC) stains: cluster of differentiation (CD) 38, CD138)

9/3/26, 4:21 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004046
13/38

Typically do not express CD19 or CD20 antigens of B-cells
Mandatory to differentiate from other small, round cell tumors

Pathology
The classic pathologic finding is sheets of neoplastic plasma cells. Plasma cells are round
cells characterized by an eccentric nucleus with an adjacent clear area (Hoffa clear zone),
which represents the prominent Golgi apparatus responsible for immunoglobulin
production. Other characteristics of plasma cells are prominent nucleolus, pale pink
cytoplasm, and a clock-face organization to the chromatin.
Special stain and IHC (CD138) aid in differentiating plasma cell neoplasms from other
small, round cell tumors, such as lymphoma.
Diagnosis
One major and one minor (or three minor) diagnostic criteria must be present.
Major criteria
Plasmacytoma: tissue diagnosis on biopsy
More than 30% plasma cells in bone marrow
Serum IgG level higher than 3.5 g/dL, IgA level higher than 2 g/dL, urine protein level higher
than 1 g/24 hours, or Bence Jones proteins
Minor criteria
10% to 30% plasma cells in bone marrow
Serum/urine protein levels lower than those listed for major criteria
Lytic bone lesions on skeletal survey
Lower-than-normal IgG level
Staging studies
Laboratory findings: normochromic, normocytic anemia; hypercalcemia; renal insufficiency;
amyloidosis; and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate
Electrophoresis: spike in serum level and/or urine protein level in 99% of patients.
Serum level: identifies types of proteins present
Urine protein level: Identifies Bence Jones proteins
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004046
14/38

Twenty-four–hour urine collection quantifies protein in urine
Beta 2 microglobulin level (>5.5 mg/L) and serum albumin level are tumor markers with
prognostic ability (increased beta 2 microglobulin level and decreased serum albumin level =
poor patient prognosis).
Bone marrow biopsy
Cytogenetic analysis correlates with patient prognosis.

Diagnosis
To establish a diagnosis of multiple myeloma, one major and one minor (or three minor)
diagnostic criteria must be present. Major criteria include plasmacytoma: tissue
diagnosis on biopsy; more than 30% plasma cells in bone marrow; and serum IgG level
higher than 3.5 g/dL, IgA level higher than 2 g/dL, urine protein level higher than 1 g/24
hour, or Bence Jones proteins. Minor criteria include 10% to 30% plasma cells in bone
marrow, serum/urine protein levels lower than those listed for major criteria, lytic bone
lesions on skeletal survey, and lower-than-normal IgG level.
Routine laboratory tests, such as a complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation
rate, or bleeding time, may prompt evaluation in asymptomatic patients. Patients with
multiple myeloma often have an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, reflecting
increased light chain production.
On diagnosis, multiple myeloma is characterized by end-organ damage, which is
remembered using the mnemonic CRAB: hypercalcemia (serum calcium level >10.5
mg/dL), renal insufficiency (creatinine level >2 mg/dL), anemia (hemoglobin level <10
g/dL), or bone lesions; however, any other sign or symptom of organ dysfunction related
to plasma cell proliferation or light chain production may qualify as a diagnostic
criterion.
After diagnosing multiple myeloma, staging studies should be performed to assess
tumor burden, patient prognosis, and myeloma-related organ and tissue impairment.
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis can identify the types of proteins present in
urine, including Bence Jones proteins.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:21 PM
AAOS | Hematopoietic Bone Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004046
15/38

Whole-body bone imaging is indicated to assess the extent of osseous involvement and
determine lesions at risk for pathologic fracture.
Bone marrow biopsy can identify the systemic nature of the disease. In addition,
cytogenetic analysis is increasingly recognized for its prognostic importance.
Markers of bone resorption (C-telopeptide, N-telopeptide, pyridinoline, and
deoxypyridinoline) and bone formation (alkaline phosphatase and osteocalcin) correlate
with skeletal-related events, progression, and survival. Other prognostic factors, such as
monoclonal protein level and serum hemoglobin, calcium, and creatinine levels, are
included in the Durie-Salmon Staging System for multiple myeloma.
Serum albumin level and beta 2 microglobulin level are additional independent
prognostic indicators that are included in the International Staging System.
Clinical features of multiple myeloma, including renal dysfunction, anemia, infection,
hyperviscosity, bleeding, or hypercalcemia, may vary widely. The prompt recognition of
these symptoms, particularly spinal cord compression, renal dysfunction, and
hypercalcemia, is critical because emergent management may prevent severe or life-
threatening complications.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Standard of care is systemic therapy.
Typically lenalidomide and bortezomib, with dexamethasone for eligible patients; often with
autologous stem cell transplantation.
Six sets of active agents for the management of multiple myeloma
Alkylating agents (melphalan, cyclophosphamide)
Anthracyclines (doxorubicin, liposomal doxorubicin)
Corticosteroids (dexamethasone, prednisone)
Immunomodulatory drugs (thalidomide, lenalidomide)
Proteosome inhibitors (bortezomib, carfilzomib)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:21 PM
AAOS | Hematopoietic Bone Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004046
16/38

Monoclonal antibodies (daratumumab, elotuzumab)
Diphosphonates or receptor activator of nuclear factor-kappa B ligand inhibitors help decrease
skeletal-related events.
Improve bone pain
Decrease serum calcium level
Especially in patients with hypercalcemia of malignancy
Radiation therapy effective to decrease pain
Emergent radiation therapy is preferred in patients who have spinal cord compression
without mechanical compromise.

Nonsurgical Management
Patients with MGUS or smoldering myeloma typically are treated via clinical observation
because the benefit of chemotherapy does not always justify the adverse effect profile.
Patients who have a solitary plasmacytoma without an elevated monoclonal protein level
can be treated via local therapy to manage the tumor and continued observation for
progression of disease. In patients with symptomatic myeloma, systemic management
should be initiated promptly on diagnosis. Induction regimens currently consist of
management with at least one novel chemotherapeutic agent for myeloma, such as
thalidomide, lenalidomide, or bortezomib. These usually are combined with a
corticosteroid and often are combined with a cytotoxic agent, such as
cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, or melphalan.
Six sets of active agents are used in the management of multiple myeloma, including
alkylating agents (melphalan, cyclophosphamide), anthracyclines (doxorubicin, liposomal
doxorubicin), corticosteroids (dexamethasone, prednisone), immunomodulatory drugs
(thalidomide, lenalidomide), proteosome inhibitors (bortezomib, carfilzomib), and
monoclonal antibodies (daratumumab, elotuzumab).
In patients younger than 65 years with a new diagnosis of multiple myeloma who do not
have precluding heart, lung, liver, or renal dysfunction, high-dose induction therapy and
autologous stem cell transplantation should be considered.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:21 PM
AAOS | Hematopoietic Bone Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004046
17/38

Given their potent anti-osteoclastic activity, bone-targeting agents, such as
diphosphonates and denosumab, are the key to decrease the risk of skeletal-related
events from myeloma bone disease. The results of some studies suggest these bone-
targeting agents also may improve overall survival.1-4 In addition, the use of bone-
targeting agents in antiresorptive therapy improves pain and symptomatic lesions and
decreases serum calcium levels. In patients with hypercalcemia of malignancy, emergent
diphosphonate treatment may be lifesaving.
Similar to most hematologic malignancies, plasmacytomas are highly radiosensitive.
External beam irradiation at a dose of 4,000 to 4,500 cGy may afford local control in
most patients with a solitary plasmacytoma. More commonly, radiation therapy is used
in the treatment of patients with spinal cord compression or painful bony lesions. In
patients who have spinal cord compression without mechanical compromise, emergent
radiation therapy is preferred; however, surgical stabilization is indicated in patients with
mechanical instability.
Surgical Management
Surgical stabilization of pathologic fractures or impending fractures
Kyphoplasty/vertebroplasty common to manage vertebral compression fractures
Postoperative radiation therapy is highly effective in patients with multiple myeloma.

Surgical Management
The role of surgical treatment is limited in patients with multiple myeloma. Although
antiresorptive therapy considerably decreases skeletal-related events in patients with
multiple myeloma, at least 5% of patients will experience a vertebral fracture. In properly
indicated patients, vertebroplasty effectively relieves pain from vertebral compression
fractures secondary to multiple myeloma. Spinal stabilization may be indicated for
unstable vertebral segments.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:21 PM
AAOS | Hematopoietic Bone Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004046
18/38

The substantial role of surgical treatment in patients with multiple myeloma involves the
management of fractures and impending pathologic fractures of the long bones, which
occur in approximately 14% of patients with multiple myeloma. Although these lesions
are overwhelmingly osteolytic, a thin sclerotic rim often develops after systemic therapy
and antiresorptive therapy, which may increase the risk of pathologic fracture. Because
no strong data suggest the contrary, myeloma bone disease typically is managed in a
manner similar to that for osteolytic skeletal metastases from carcinomas.
Patients with a bone fracture and patients at risk for fracture from normal activity are
surgical candidates for stabilization. Because multiple myeloma is a systemic disease
that is extremely sensitive to radiation therapy, the complete removal of neoplastic cells
from the lesion during fixation generally is not necessary. After stabilization, which
typically is achieved with the use of an intramedullary nail or a cortical plate and screws,
the affected bone can be effectively managed via radiation therapy. Large skeletal
defects often benefit from curettage and a combination of polymethyl methacrylate and
metal used to augment fixation, which afford adequate stability to allow for immediate
weight bearing.
Complications
Skeletal-related events
Pathologic fracture
Need for surgical stabilization
Need for radiation therapy
Spinal cord compression
Hypercalcemia of malignancy
As high as 30% in patients with multiple myeloma
Renal insufficiency
Hyperviscosity
Increased risk for venous thromboembolism
Complications of antiresorptive therapy (diphosphonates and receptor activator of nuclear
factor-kappa B ligand inhibitors)
Osteonecrosis of the jaw
Atypical stress fractures
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:21 PM
AAOS | Hematopoietic Bone Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004046
19/38


Complications
Skeletal complications of multiple myeloma typically are described as skeletal-related
events. These include pathologic fracture, The need for surgical stabilization, the need
for radiation therapy, spinal cord compression, and hypercalcemia of malignancy.
Hypercalcemia will develop in approximately 30% of patients with multiple myeloma and
may result in a medical emergency. Potential symptoms of hypercalcemia include
confusion, cardiac arrhythmias, and renal insufficiency. Urgent hydration and
intravenous zoledronic acid treatment should be initiated in patients with hypercalcemia
resulting from multiple myeloma. Given the high rate of renal dysfunction in patients
with advanced multiple myeloma, dose adjustments of diphosphonates may be
necessary.
Multiple myeloma may affect several organ systems, which may result in considerable
perioperative complications. Myeloma-associated anemia usually can be controlled via
erythropoiesis-stimulating agents; however, transfusion may be necessary for
procedures in which moderate volumes of blood loss are expected. Thrombotic
complications and the risk for hyperviscosity syndrome are considerably increased in
this patient population. Patients with multiple myeloma also have an increased risk for
infection.
Patients who undergo antiresorptive therapy have an increased risk for osteonecrosis of
the jaw and atypical stress fractures. Dose adjustment may mitigate the risk of stress
fractures. A preoperative dental consultation and the completion of all invasive dental
work before antiresorptive therapy may mitigate the risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw.
Outcomes
Drastic improvement in survival in the past 10 years
Patient prognosis is associated with the following:
Cytogenetic profile
Serum albumin level (3.5 g/dL)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:21 PM
AAOS | Hematopoietic Bone Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004046
20/38

Serum beta 2 microglobulin level (<3.5 mg/L, 3.5 to 5.5 mg/dL, or >5.5 mg/dL)
Risk stratification of patients allows for individualized treatment.
Some improved survival after early or late autologous stem cell transplantation
Survival poorer in patients with renal failure
Median survival is 8 years (prognosis and treatment more individualized).

Outcomes
Overall, the survival of patients with multiple myeloma has drastically improved in the
past 10 years. Patient prognosis is associated with the cytogenetic profile and serum
laboratory values.
Primary Lymphoma of Bone
Overview
Definition and demographics
A neoplasm composed of malignant lymphoid cells, producing one or more masses within
bone
Most primary lymphomas of bone are non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphomas.
Comprises 7% of all malignant bone tumors
Occurs in males more than females
Can occur in all age groups.
Most common in patients aged 35 to 55 years

Overview
According to the World Health Organization, primary lymphoma of bone is a neoplasm
composed of malignant lymphoid cells, producing one or more masses within bone
without any supra-regional lymph node involvement or other extranodal lesions.

Lymphomas are divided into two categories based on specific histologic and cytogenetic
features: Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is
further characterized based on presumed lymphocytic cell of origin. These often are
further subclassified based on prognostic factors and location of involvement.
Epidemiology
Primary lymphoma of bone is exceedingly rare.
Occurs if no extra-skeletal sites of disease (other than a single node) is present for 6 months
after diagnosis
50% of patients are older than 40 years.
Most primary bone lymphomas are diffuse large B-cell lymphomas.

Epidemiology
Primary lymphoma of bone is not a common disease, comprising approximately 7% of
all malignant bone tumors, 5% of all extranodal lymphomas, and less than 1% of all non-
Hodgkin lymphomas.
In contrast, primary nodal lymphomas frequently involve the skeletal system, with bone
involvement observed in 16% to 20% of patients.
Anatomic Considerations
Frequently occur in the femur followed by the pelvis, vertebrae, and humerus
Usually arising in the metaphyseal region of long bones, such as the femur (Figure 4),
humerus, and tibia
In general, the skeletal distribution tends to follow areas of increased hematopoietic activity.
Approximately 10% to 40% of cases are multifocal, producing several lesions in one bone or
involving multiple bones concurrently (polyostotic)

May be difficult to diagnose on needle biopsy because the tissue is susceptible to crushing
An open biopsy may be required for adequate tissue.
Biopsy from soft-tissue component is preferred, if present.
A frozen section is obtained to ensure diagnostic tissue is present.
Adequate amount of tissue must be obtained for ancillary techniques, including
immunophenotyping, flow cytometry, fluorescent in situ hybridization, and polymerase chain
reaction.
The specimen should be handled gently and placed in normal saline, not Formalin.

Mixed small, round blue cell infiltrate (different sizes and shapes; Figure 5)
Diffuse infiltrative rather than nodular pattern

Biopsy Principles and Pathology Guidelines
Pathology in lymphoma is characterized by sheets of neoplastic round cells. Because this
may be a mixed cell infiltrate, infection and other round cell tumors (Ewing sarcoma)
often are included in the differential diagnosis.

Gentle and appropriate handling of the biopsy specimen is critical in patients with
lymphoma because the cells are sensitive to crush artifact. Open biopsy may be required
to attain adequate volume of specimen and to avoid cell injury. Biopsy from the soft-
tissue component of bone lesion may contain more diagnostic tissue and avoid the
mechanical cell injury that can occur during biopsy of the osseous component.
The specimen should be sent fresh, without formalin, to allow for the multiple IHC tests
required for diagnosis and to subclassify lymphoma.
Most lymphomas of bone are non-Hodgkins B cell lymphoma and have the IHC profile of
CD20+, CD45+, and lymphocyte common antigen positive. Negative IHC testing (CD138,
CD99) may aid in eliminating other round cell tumors in the differential diagnosis.
Prognosis
Primary lymphoma of bone is associated with a better prognosis than secondary involvement
of bone in lymphoma.
Age often is correlated with survival, with patients 60 years or younger having a better survival
rate.

Prognosis
Current treatment protocols (combination of chemotherapy and radiation therapy) yield
overall survival rates greater than 90%.

Constant pain unrelieved by rest
A large soft-tissue mass that is tender or warm is common.
Lymphomas affect bones with persistent red marrow (femur, spine, pelvis).

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
The lesions observed on MRI usually have a poorly defined border with extensive
marrow edema (Figure 9, A). In general, a high signal intensity is observed on T2-

show varying amounts of cortical destruction and periosteal reaction. Lymphoma of

occasionally may be greater than the bony component.

Biopsy
Biopsy is the preferred method for diagnosis.
Differential Diagnosis
Metastasis of unknown primary origin
Osteomyelitis
Langerhans cell histiocytosis
Other malignant tumors (primary or secondary) in bone (osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma,
carcinomas, and leukemia)
Clinical features (age, location) in combination with a detailed patient history and physical
examination is preferred.
In most patients, a pathologist using a broad panel of IHC markers should easily differentiate
between these entities.
Langerhans cell histiocytosis can be easily ruled out on representative biopsy material via
negative CD1a, Langerin, and S100 IHC.
If IHC for CD20 and PAX5 fails to demonstrate atypical large B cells, morphology with
edematous stroma and a reactive infiltrate may reflect chronic osteomyelitis.
If the patient is older than 50 years, metastasis from primary carcinoma is a serious
differential diagnosis, as is Ewing sarcoma in a young patient.
In patients with carcinoma (keratin positive, lymphoma markers negative), additional markers
to determine the primary origin of carcinoma should be performed5 (Table 1).

Management
Medical Management
Multiagent chemotherapy with or without local irradiation
For non-Hodgkin lymphoma, systemic chemotherapy regimens with prednisone
(cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone), is the preferred protocol.
Immune-modulating antibody, known as rituximab, has been added to the standard
protocol).
For Hodgkin lymphoma, traditional cytotoxic chemotherapeutic agents (doxorubicin,
bleomycin, vincristine, and dacarbazine) continue to be used.
These agents alter the immune system and increase infection risk.

Medical Management
Rituximab is a monoclonal chimeric antibody directed at the B-cell antigen CD20, which
is expressed in 95% of non-Hodgkin lymphomas. Rituximab is added to systemic therapy
regimens, with multiple studies reporting improvements in patients overall and disease-
free survival.6,7
Infection is a great concern inpatients treated via systemic therapy regimens with
rituximab or other chemotherapy protocols. Therefore, if patients are treated via these
regimens shortly postoperatively, the risk of infection of metallic implants is a concern.
Patients should be monitored closely during early wound healing if they are undergoing
chemotherapy.
Local irradiation
Radiation therapy may be added to attain local control in patients with persistent
disease.
Although radiation therapy was historically included in the treatment paradigm,
uncertainty remains with regard to whether radiation therapy improves outcomes in
the era of antibody therapy and chemotherapy.
Large, prospective studies are necessary to definitively establish whether radiation
therapy is necessary in the treatment of patients with lymphoma of bone.
Surgical Management
Establish the diagnosis8 (Resource 4)
Obtaining an adequate tissue sample is preferred for making the pathologic diagnosis of
lymphoma.
Manage impending or actual pathologic fractures
The surgeon should aim to stabilize lesions at risk for fracture before an actual fracture
occurs (similar to principles for metastatic disease).
If a fracture occurs, surgical management and postoperative recovery are more difficult in
this patient population.

Summary
Orthopedic surgeons commonly are involved in the diagnosis and management of patients with
myeloma and lymphoma. The ultimate goals of orthopaedic management are accurate diagnosis,
improved function, and decreased pain. Pathologic fractures are common and should be
prevented if possible.
Coordinated care with radiation therapy and medical oncology is imperative in the treatment of
patients with myeloma or lymphoma. Any patient with unexplained bone pain should be
thoughtfully evaluated by an orthopedic surgeon to prevent delayed diagnosis of an underlying
malignancy.
